findings.headline: Local elections in 2027 may impair ability to make difficult spending decisions
findings.detail: The prospect of local elections in 2027 and the lead-up will inevitably present Members with challenges in making difficult decisions. The review notes that given the financial pressures arising from changes in pooled budgets and reliance on transformation being delivered, it is difficult to see how the council can avoid further applications for EFS or further diminution of reserves.
findings.matters: Electoral cycles create political headwinds for difficult decisions (service cuts, workforce reductions). The timing of Somerset's elections, combined with ongoing financial stress, may slow the pace of decisions needed to achieve the transformation plan.
findings.figures: Local elections 2027
findings.quote: The prospect of local elections in 2027 and the lead up will inevitably present Members with challenges in making more difficult decisions. Given the financial pressures arising with change in pooled budgets and the reliance on transformation plans being delivered, it is difficult to see that further application for EFS/further diminution of reserves can easily be avoided.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) Somerset External Assurance Review 2026 , item 28.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s68883/Appendix 2 Ministry of Housing Communities and Local Government MHCLG Somerset External Assuran.pdf
findings.headline: Capital programme underperformance: £17.95m underspend in 2025-26 due to poor delivery
findings.detail: Poor performance in delivering the capital programme for 2025-26 resulted in a £17.95m underspend in Treasury Management. The council's budget had assumed full capital programme delivery, so the actual underspend masked underlying revenue pressure. The interim S151 Officer has undertaken a detailed review to establish more realistic capital funding requirements for 2026-27 onwards.
findings.matters: Repeated capital programme underspends signal either over-optimism in planning or delivery capability weakness. They mask underlying revenue pressure (budgets built on assumed capital activity that doesn't happen), leading to false reporting of outturn.
findings.figures: £17.95m Treasury Management underspend from poor capital programme delivery in 2025-26
findings.quote: Poor performance in delivering the capital programme for 2025-26 resulted in £17.95 million underspend in Treasury Management. The capital programme has now been subject to a detailed review based on more prudent assumptions in relation to borrowing requirements and delivery and amended for 2026-27 onwards in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS).

findings.headline: Company financial risks: Red Brick (Life Factory), Opium, Gravity requiring management and shareholder oversight
findings.detail: The council holds interests in three companies with financial and governance risks. Red Brick (Life Factory) has already triggered an external auditor Statutory Recommendation due to council failures in governance. Opium requires further investment to secure its trading future. Gravity's revised commercial model is being finalised with the Department of Business and Trade. The council is establishing Shareholder Committee arrangements to provide oversight.

Ongoing requirements to invest in Opium, and complex negotiations around Gravity, add financial uncertainty and require active management.

findings.quote: In the S151 Officer's Section 25 statement for 2026-27, there is comment about the exposure the council has in relation to its role as Accountable Body and company issues including the following issues: a) Red Brick (Life Factory) - where the External Auditor has already issued a Statutory Recommendation in relation to failures by the council.

findings.headline: Asset disposal programme fragmented; may reduce capital receipts available to fund transformation
findings.detail: Asset management and the asset disposal programme are currently split between operational property and commercial assets, with no single point of contact or corporate landlord model. This fragmentation may reduce the ability to deliver the capital receipts needed to fund the transformation programme. The review recommends a single focused team.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a core funding route for the transformation programme and capitalisation direction. If the asset disposal programme underperforms, the council loses both the capital receipts and the revenue return (through ongoing maintenance/operational cost savings) that transformed assets would deliver.
findings.figures: No specific numbers; fragmentation identified as a risk to capital receipts delivery
findings.quote: Asset management and the management of the asset disposal programmes are currently fragmented which may reduce the ability to deliver the capital receipts that will fund transformation therefore a single focussed team would reduce the risk of this having a detrimental impact on the council's progress to financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Transformation ROI shortfall: £20.58m return on £15.31m invested (1.34:1) versus 3:1 target
findings.detail: Current transformation investments of £15.313m are forecast to yield only £20.580m (1.34:1 return), falling significantly short of the intended 3:1 return. To achieve 3:1 return would require £135m in financial benefits over the MTFP. Strategic partner (Newton Europe) involvement is expected to help but carries costs up to £20m.
findings.matters: The transformation programme is the stated solution to financial sustainability. If the current projects only deliver 1.34:1 return when 3:1 is required, the programme is not delivering the assumed savings, and the gap to balance widens.
findings.figures: Current investments £15.313m forecast yield £20.580m (1.34:1); target 3:1 requiring £135m benefits; strategic partner cost up to £20m
findings.quote: At the time that the budget was set the current total investments of £15.313 million are forecast to yield £20.580 million over the MTFP period which is a proposed rate of return of 1.34:1 which is lower than the expectation of 3:1.

findings.headline: Underlying 2025-26 position: £37m overspend masked by one-off measures and capitalisation
findings.detail: The draft 2025-26 outturn shows a net underspend of £6.342m, but this includes a £43m capitalisation request. The underlying position is a net overspend of £37m. Service budgets overspent net £1.547m, with Children's Services £11.362m over, though Adult Services underspent £8.221m due to underfunding.
findings.matters: The reported underspend is illusory: without capitalisation (which mortgages future revenue), the council is spending £37m more than it receives. This is the real position that must be funded by EFS, reserves, or savings.
findings.figures: Reported underspend £6.342m; underlying overspend £37m before capitalisation; Children's Services £11.362m over
findings.quote: This outturn position for 2025-26 and the resulting net underspend does take account of the request from the council for £43 million in capitalisation which means that the underlying position is a net overspend of £37 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) Somerset External Assurance Review 2026 , item 28.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s68883/Appendix 2 Ministry of Housing Communities and Local Government MHCLG Somerset External Assuran.pdf
findings.headline: 2026-27 funding gap £25m; MTFP gap £88.368m before EFS
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget shows a funding gap of £25m before EFS, rising to £88.368m across the medium term. The budget has been balanced only through one-off resources including EFS and unplanned Collection Fund surplus. The S151 Officer stated this approach "does not provide a sustainable solution and increases financial risk in future years."
findings.matters: A multi-year funding gap of this scale, dependent on continued EFS and one-offs, is unsustainable. The gap grows each year, signalling structural imbalance between spend and revenue that transformation is not yet closing at the required pace.
findings.figures: 2026-27 funding gap £25m; MTFP gap £88.368m before EFS
findings.quote: The 2026-27 budget includes a funding gap before Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £25.000 million, increasing to £88.368 million across the medium term, reflecting sustained demand and cost pressures across key statutory services, particularly children's social care, adult social care and Special Education Needs and Disabilities (SEND). The budget for 2026-27 has been balanced only through the use of one-off resources, including Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) and an unplanned Collection Fund surplus. This approach does not provide a sustainable solution and increases financial risk in future years.

findings.headline: Finance system (Microsoft Dynamics) not fully functional and contributing to management weakness
findings.detail: The core finance system, Microsoft Dynamics, is not fully functional. It is not one of the most commonly used systems of its type. The finance team capacity and capability review noted that there are only a small number of fully qualified accountants at senior level, limited staff rotation, and resilience issues with skills resting on individual officers.
findings.matters: A non-functional finance system impairs visibility into real-time financial position and increases the risk of undetected overspends. Combined with a small cadre of qualified staff and no contingency depth, this is a control weakness that directly affects financial reliability.
findings.figures: Finance and Procurement team ~164 FTE; small number of qualified accountants at senior level; finance system not fully functional
findings.quote: The current structure covering Finance and Procurement has approximately 164 FTE and whilst the finance team is regarded as having more FTE than it needs, this was deemed to be a consequence of a number of factors. a) There are only a small number of fully qualified accountants at the more senior level b) The finance system is not fully functional c) There has not been a comprehensive review and rationalisation of all processes

findings.headline: Four changes in Section 151 Officer since April 2023; permanent appointment taking up post July 2026
findings.detail: The council has experienced four changes in the S151 Officer (Chief Finance Officer) since the unitary was formed in April 2023, creating instability in financial leadership, style and approach. An interim postholder has been in place since June 2025 and extended to March 2027, but a substantive appointment was made to take up post in late July 2026.
findings.matters: Frequent turnover in the s151 role is red flag for lenders. It signals either instability in the role itself or difficulty recruiting/retaining qualified people in a distressed position. The interim arrangement has limited duration and dependent on recruitment success.
findings.figures: Four s151 changes in three years (April 2023-2026)
findings.quote: There have been four changes in the S151 Officer since April 2023 which has created instability in terms of the style and approach, and the implementation of a new core finance system (Microsoft Dynamics) that is not one of the most popularly used systems of its type, have also had some impact on the financial management of the council.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s68883/Appendix 2 Ministry of Housing Communities and Local Government MHCLG Somerset External Assuran.pdf
findings.headline: SEND High Needs deficit escalating: £217m by 2028 without grant support
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block deficit is rising sharply: £61.993m actual 2024-25, £116.8m 2025-26, £174.107m 2026-27, and £217.229m projected 2027-28. Without the High Needs Stability Grant, the deficit would reach £217.229m by 31 March 2028. The statutory override ringfencing this deficit expires March 2028, after which it hits the General Fund.
findings.matters: A growing SEND deficit is a liability clock: it accrues each year and falls back to the General Fund when the statutory override ends in March 2028. Even with the stability grant assumption, the council is betting on DfE providing a further 90% grant in each of the next two years—a dependency, not a control.
findings.quote: Without the new High Needs Stability Grant (HNSG), covering 90% of their High Needs Block only related Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit accrued up to 2025-26, by 31 March 2028, the deficit would increase to £116.800 million by March 2026 and £217.229 million by 31 March 2028.

findings.headline: Children Looked After numbers rising; placement sufficiency a significant financial risk
findings.detail: Children Looked After numbers rose from 604 in October 2024 to 701 in March 2026 (97 additional children). Demand entering the system exceeds throughput. External residential placements (which carry substantially higher unit costs than foster placements) are increasing materially. The review found limited evidence that placement growth has stabilised.
findings.matters: Rising CLA numbers, especially in high-cost external placements, create direct revenue pressure that compounds the existing overspend. The review notes workforce is not growing proportionately to demand (33% demand growth), creating agency dependency and further cost pressure.
findings.figures: CLA numbers 604 (Oct 2024) to 701 (March 2026); 33% demand growth without proportionate staffing increase
findings.quote: Children Looked After numbers increased from 604 in October 2024 to 701 in March 2026. Usage of homes and hostels placements, children's homes and external residential [placements increase]. The increase in residential placements is materially significant from a financial perspective. External residential placements typically carry substantially higher unit costs than foster placements and increase financial volatility within Children's Services budgets.

findings.headline: Children's Services expenditure 16.2% above peer councils; theoretical variance of £34.3m against best performers
findings.detail: Somerset's Children's Social Care spend per child aged 0-17 is 16.2% above nearest neighbour averages. Expenditure on Children Looked After (CLA) is 27.1% above peers, and safeguarding spend is 32% above comparators. Benchmarking identifies a theoretical notional variance of £34.3m if the council matched top comparators.
findings.matters: Children's Services is driving material overspends. The council's own figures show 2025-26 Children's Services overspent by £11.362m. The scale of the spend differential signals either inefficiency in service delivery or structural placement/demand issues that transformation has not yet addressed.
findings.figures: 16.2% above neighbour average; 27.1% above on CLA; 32% above on safeguarding; £34.3m theoretical variance to best performer
findings.quote: Somerset's Children's Social Care expenditure per child aged 0–17 is 16.2% above nearest neighbour averages, ranking 4th highest within the comparator group. Expenditure relating specifically to Children Looked After (CLA) is 27.1% above nearest neighbour averages, whilst safeguarding expenditure is 32% above comparator averages. The benchmarking analysis also identifies a theoretical notional variance of £34.3 million against top comparator performance levels within Children's Social Care.

findings.headline: Transformation programme not delivering planned savings; £40m of EFS funding not yet released
findings.detail: Of the £120m EFS received, £40m was allocated to fund transformation delivery. The transformation has been reprofiled and aside from some staffing reductions, significant service delivery transformation remains unachieved. The review notes the pace of delivery is not sufficient to deliver planned cost reductions.
findings.matters: The council's financial recovery plan rests on transformation delivering specified savings. If the £40m earmarked for transformation does not translate to realised cost reductions, the gap to sustainability widens and the need for further EFS or capitalisation grows.
findings.figures: £40m of £120m EFS allocated to transformation; pace of delivery assessed as insufficient
findings.quote: £40m of the EFS of £120 million over three years was to support the delivery of transformation which has thus far not been delivered as planned. Transformation plans have been reprofiled however aside from some reduction in the staffing pay-bill there is still a significant amount of service delivery transformation to be achieved.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves £6.9m below the minimum prudent level
findings.detail: At 31 March 2026, General Fund reserves of £67.363m fall short of the S151 Officer's assessed 10% of net revenue budget (£74.252m) by £6.889m. The council has low resilience to withstand financial distress. The gap needs to be replenished over the MTFP.
findings.matters: Reserves below prudent levels signal vulnerability to service volatility, demand shocks, or further transformation delays. A lender needs confidence that the council has buffers to absorb bad news.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve £67.363m; required level £74.252m; shortfall £6.889m
findings.quote: At 31st March 2026, the General Fund reserve of £67.363 million is £ 6.889 million less than the risk based 10% of the net revenue budget which means there is limited resilience to withstand further financial distress.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s68883/Appendix 2 Ministry of Housing Communities and Local Government MHCLG Somerset External Assuran.pdf
findings.headline: Council Tax increase request refused; EFS dependency entering fourth year
findings.detail: Somerset sought permission to raise Council Tax above 4.99% without referendum for 2026-27 and capitalisation direction, but the tax rise was refused. The council has received almost £120m of EFS over three years. The capitalisation direction was successful but the council remains dependent on extraordinary support.
findings.matters: A lender evaluating sustainability needs to know that the council's own revenue base cannot absorb the spending pressures without government emergency support, and that the government has begun refusing even the council's requests.
findings.figures: £120 million EFS over three years; 2026-27 tax rise request refused; capitalisation direction approved
findings.quote: Somerset Council submitted its Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) application for 2026-27 seeking permission to raise Council Tax for a second year above 4.99% without the need for a referendum in addition to a capitalisation direction. This was the third consecutive year of a request for EFS reprofiling existing support from previous year primarily to fund transformation and for 2026-27 the increase in Council Tax was refused however the capitalisation direction was successful.

findings.headline: Financial position remains fragile and dependent on EFS despite 2026/27 progress

findings.headline: HRA capital programme pushing debt servicing costs from 10% to 18% of net income over MTFP period
findings.detail: While the Housing Revenue Account is described as 'in a positive place', the council warns that the scale of the capital programme is pushing debt servicing costs as a proportion of net income from 10% to 18% over the medium term. findings.matters: Rising debt servicing costs constrain HRA financial flexibility. Any rise in interest rates or refinancing costs could force either capital programme cuts or HRA rent increases, which are politically sensitive.

findings.detail: The external auditor has issued three Statutory Recommendations in the 2024/25 Auditor Annual Report relating to setting a balanced budget, delivery of transformation, and the Council's role as Accountable Body for the Town Deal. Statutory Recommendations are 'the most serious form of recommendation' after a Public Interest Report and 'must be address promptly and diligently'.
findings.matters: Statutory Recommendations indicate the external auditor has formal concerns about the council's financial management and governance. This signals audit-identified risks that require disclosure and remediation.
findings.figures: Three Statutory Recommendations issued for 2024/25
findings.quote: With the exception of a Public Interest Report, Statutory Recommendations are the most serious form of recommendation and must be address promptly and diligently.

findings.headline: Maintained school deficits rising with most schools forecasting in-year shortfalls
findings.detail: Rising deficits across maintained schools with 'most schools now forecasting in year deficits and cumulative shortfalls increasing year on year'. Local authorities cannot write off these deficits using reserves. The report warns that 'Failure to stabilise schools' finances will increase pressure on the local authority balance sheet and heighten financial risks across the wider education and SEND system in Somerset'.
findings.matters: School deficits represent a growing contingent liability on the council balance sheet. While technically schools' problems, the council must ultimately absorb deficits that cannot be funded from school balances.
findings.figures: Most maintained schools forecasting in-year deficits; cumulative shortfalls increasing year on year
findings.quote: Rising deficits across maintained schools reflect a significantly worsening financial position, with most schools now forecasting in year deficits and cumulative shortfalls increasing year on year... findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63336/Report of the S151 Officer Section 25 Statement.pdf
findings.headline: Explicit statutory risk of Section 114 notice if council cannot set a balanced lawful budget in future years
findings.detail: The S151 Officer explicitly warns that failure to address key risks 'could compromise the Council's ability to set a balanced and lawful budget in future years. If this occurs, the Council may be required to issue a Section 114 notice. Such a position would have severe operational and financial consequences and would limit local discretion over service and financial decision making.' Both principal strategic risks (Medium Term Financial Sustainability and SEND escalation) are scored at the maximum risk level of 25 (very high).
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice would impose external control, block most discretionary spending, and substantially increase credit risk. It signals the council is no longer in financial control.
findings.figures: Strategic risks ORG0009 and ORG011 both at maximum score of 25 (very high/critical likelihood and impact)
findings.quote: Failure to bring demand under control, deliver approved savings and drive transformation at the required scale places the Council at serious risk of being unable to set a balanced budget in future years. If this occurs, the Council may be required to issue a Section 114 notice. Such a position would have severe operational and financial consequences and would limit local discretion over service and financial decision making.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63336/Report of the S151 Officer Section 25 Statement.pdf
findings.headline: Transformation programme must deliver £135m savings by 2031 but pace and credibility at risk
findings.detail: The entire financial recovery plan depends on the transformation programme delivering a minimum of £135m of savings by 31 March 2031 (with 3:1 return on investment). However, the S151 Officer identifies 'risk that the current lack of pace and shortage of suitably transformative and ambitious scheme proposals could result in this target not being met'. The report emphasises 'The importance of identifying opportunities and moving more quickly from governance to delivery cannot be stressed enough'.
findings.matters: If transformation slips, the council has no alternative mechanism to close the structural budget gap. This is a critical path item for financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £135m savings target by 31 March 2031; 3:1 return on investment required; medium-term gap £88.368m by 2031
findings.quote: In order to achieve the necessary Return on Investment of 3:1 by 31 March 2031, the programme needs to identify and deliver a minimum of £135m of savings and at present there remains a risk that the current lack of pace and shortage of suitably transformative and ambitious scheme proposals could result in this target not being met.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63336/Report of the S151 Officer Section 25 Statement.pdf
findings.headline: Council Tax flexibility exhausted—request to raise above 4.99% cap was refused
findings.detail: Somerset sought government permission to increase Council Tax above the national limit of 4.99% without a referendum, but was refused. The S151 Officer states this 'option is now effectively closed to the Council for future years'. Combined with exhaustion of Exceptional Financial Support, this leaves the council dependent on service reduction or transformation to close budget gaps.
findings.matters: Loss of Council Tax flexibility removes a potential lever for budget balance. With EFS unlikely to continue and Council Tax capped, the council is forced into service cuts or ambitious transformation with no room for error.
findings.figures: Council Tax increase limit 4.99%; request to exceed cap refused
findings.quote: Having sought and been refused permission to raise Council Tax above the nationally stipulated of 4.99% without a referendum, this option is now effectively closed to the Council for future years.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63336/Report of the S151 Officer Section 25 Statement.pdf
findings.headline: Structural loss of £20.955m annual funding from removal of 'Remoteness' factor in Fair Funding formula from 2028/29
findings.detail: The new Fair Funding formula removes the 'Remoteness' weighting for all services except Adult Social Care. For Somerset, a rural authority with nearly 50% of population in rural areas, this represents a permanent annual loss of £20.955m from 2028/29 onwards, equal to 3.2% of Core Spending Power and 'the third largest reduction in cash terms' nationally. This loss comes with no equivalent reduction in statutory obligations.
findings.matters: This is a structural, permanent, government-imposed funding cut with no mitigation available to the council. It widens the structural budget gap and represents lost financial capacity in a council already facing medium-term deficits.
findings.figures: £20.955m annual loss from 2028/29; equals 3.2% of Core Spending Power; third largest cash loss nationally
findings.quote: It is estimated that Somerset Council will be losing £20.955m in a full year (from 2028/29) from the removal of this factor in the calculation - the third largest reduction in cash terms and equal to 3.2% of Core Spending Power.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report

findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs rising unsustainably and described as unaffordable
findings.detail: Number of children looked after has risen steadily, case complexity has increased, and average placement costs are rising. The S151 Officer states these factors are 'leading to significant overspends every year that cannot be sustained'. The service is instructed to 'look to best in class authorities to adopt new social work practices' but no specific savings plan is detailed.
findings.matters: Placement overspends in a core statutory service are explicitly characterised as unsustainable. This is the single largest source of in-year pressure (Q3 2025/26 overspend £6.367m total, with children's services a material part).
findings.figures: Q3 2025/26 service overspend £6.367m; without Capitalisation Direction would be £42.901m (5.35% of budget)
findings.quote: The number of children looked after by Somerset Council has risen steadily over the last two years and the complexity of cases has become a major factor for the service. The average cost of external placements also is increasing, and all these factors are leading to significant overspends every year that cannot be sustained

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63336/Report of the S151 Officer Section 25 Statement.pdf
findings.headline: SEND deficit escalating to £208.205m by 2027/28 with only partial government funding and ongoing uncertainty
findings.detail: High Needs Block deficit forecast at £116.800m for 2025/26, cumulative DSG deficit reaching £107.775m by March 2026 and rising to £208.205m by 2027/28. Government is providing High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of deficits up to March 2026 (£105.120m), but the council must fund the remaining 10% (£11.680m). Support for new deficits in 2027/28 and 2028/29 'remains uncertain, with potential additional exposure of £100.430m'. The statutory override protecting the General Fund from DSG deficits expires 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: The S151 Officer identifies this as 'the most significant existential risk to the Council'. SEND deficits will hit the General Fund directly after 2028, and the council has no control over demand (EHCP rising caseloads are driven by national entitlements).
findings.figures: £116.800m HNB deficit 2025/26; £208.205m cumulative DSG deficit by 2027/28; £105.120m government grant (90%); £11.680m council contribution required; £100.430m potential additional exposure
findings.quote: the High Needs Block (HNB) deficit presents arguably the most significant existential risk to the Council and delivery of the Deficit Management Plan remains critical, as the deficit will continue to escalate unless the planned actions are implemented in full and at the required pace.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63336/Report of the S151 Officer Section 25 Statement.pdf
findings.headline: General Fund reserves £11m below recommended target and explicitly described as vulnerable
findings.detail: Current General Fund balance is £63.200m against a recommended risk-based target of £74.252m (10% of net revenue budget for 2026/27). The S151 Officer states reserves 'remain at a lower level than required given the risks faced by the Council' and 'must be rebuilt over the medium term to improve financial resilience and reduce reliance on exceptional support'.

findings.quote: The General Fund balance of £63.200m remains below the recommended risk-based target of 10% of net revenue budget, equivalent to £74.252m for 2026/27... the General Fund balance is vulnerable and must be rebuilt over the medium term to improve financial resilience and reduce reliance on exceptional support.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63336/Report of the S151 Officer Section 25 Statement.pdf
findings.headline: £25m funding gap for 2026/27 closed only with exceptional government support now in its third consecutive year
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget has been balanced using Exceptional Financial Support of £25.000m and an unplanned Collection Fund surplus of £16.048m. The Section 151 Officer explicitly warns this approach 'does not provide a sustainable solution and increases financial risk in future years', and notes 'it is unlikely that MHCLG would entertain a fourth' year of such exceptional support.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's budget is not sustainably balanced and depends on discretionary government support with no path to core balance. A fourth year request would likely trigger external intervention.
findings.figures: £25.000m Exceptional Financial Support, £16.048m Collection Fund surplus; medium-term gap increases to £88.368m by 2030/31
findings.quote: The budget for 2026/27 has been balanced only through the use of one-off resources, including Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) and an unplanned Collection Fund surplus. This approach does not provide a sustainable solution and increases financial risk in future years.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget 2026/27, Council Tax 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27-2030/31
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63304/Revenue and Capital Budget 2026-27 Council Tax 2026-27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 -.pdf
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer warns council remains in 'deeply fragile' financial position despite budget approval, with ongoing reliance on exceptional support unavoidable
findings.detail: The Interim Chief Finance Officer states in the budget narrative that 'the Council's financial position remains deeply fragile' despite two years of Financial Emergency controls and an integrated council structure. The S151 Officer confirms reliance on one-off measures remains 'unavoidable at this stage' and warns that without sustained transformation and cost reduction, the council cannot move to sustainable balance.
findings.matters: The Section 151 Officer's assessment is the statutory baseline for council financial health. An assessment of 'deeply fragile' position with unavoidable reliance on one-off support is a red flag for lenders and rating agencies.
findings.figures: £25.000m EFS in 2026/27; £75.884m approved EFS across 2024/25-2026/27 (with repurposing of 2025/26 allocation)
findings.quote: Although some of the additional controls have been stepped down or relaxed since then, the Council's financial position remains deeply fragile... Somerset Council has required a third year of Exceptional Financial Support to produce a balanced budget in 2026/27. Despite savings already identified and ongoing work to reduce the structural deficit, the scale of the financial challenge means that one-off measures remain unavoidable at this stage.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget 2026/27, Council Tax 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27-2030/31
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63304/Revenue and Capital Budget 2026-27 Council Tax 2026-27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 -.pdf
findings.headline: Transformation programme targets £135m savings over five years but delivery depends on spending £45m through Newton Europe partnership with unproven results
findings.detail: The council is committing £45m to a transformation programme through Newton Europe to deliver a 3:1 savings-to-investment ratio (£135m savings by March 2031). The MTFP depends on transformation delivering £8.051m of the £21.836m total 2026/27 savings, rising each year. However, the council has no track record of large-scale transformation delivering at scale, and the Interim Chief Finance Officer warns 'continued failure to get a financial grip in these areas will severely impact' budget balance.
findings.matters: The savings plan is heavily dependent on transformation delivery that has not yet been demonstrated. If Newton-led initiatives underdeliver, the structural gap widens and the council will need further EFS or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £45.000m transformation investment; £135.000m target savings by March 2031; 3:1 ratio required; £8.051m transformation savings in 2026/27 total; £45.873m total capitalised transformation costs
findings.quote: To deliver the Inspiring Innovation Transformation programme, £45m has been allocated through the capital programme, funded through current and future provision of Capital Receipts. All investment under the Inspiring Innovation Transformation Programme is subject to achieving a 3:1 savings-to-investment ratio, to achieve the necessary Return on Investment by 31st March 2031, the programme needs to deliver a minimum of £135m of savings.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget 2026/27, Council Tax 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27-2030/31
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63304/Revenue and Capital Budget 2026-27 Council Tax 2026-27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 -.pdf
findings.headline: Social care provider market described as 'extremely fragile' due to wage inflation and employer NICs, driving costs beyond budgeted inflation
findings.detail: The council's Adult Social Care budget faces pressure from provider cost inflation exceeding the assumed rate. The market is 'extremely fragile' due to National Living Wage increases and Employers' National Insurance Contribution rises, which providers are passing through to councils. The council is also seeing an increasing number of self-funded clients becoming eligible for local authority support, adding unpredictable demand.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is the largest demand-driven service. Market fragility and contractual inflation passing through faster than budgeted threatens 2026/27 delivery and future MTFP assumptions.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care growth request £10.597m (2026/27), growing to £13.763m (2030/31); inflation (non-contractual) £9.948m (2026/27) across all services

findings.headline: General Fund reserves below minimum recommended level, limiting capacity to absorb financial shocks
findings.detail: The council's General Fund balance stands at £63.2m, which is 85% of the 10% appropriate level and £11.052m below the minimum 5% risk-based level of £37.126m. The Section 151 Officer has warned this shortfall must be addressed over the MTFP period. With a Q3 2025/26 overspend of £6.367m already reported, the council has limited buffer if in-year pressures emerge.
findings.matters: Weak reserves leave the council unable to handle demand shocks or savings slippage. The Q3 overspend shows recurring control issues; a similar 2026/27 performance would materially worsen solvency.

findings.headline: Underlying structural budget gap of £39.048m in 2026/27 after removing one-off items, recurring in future years
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget is balanced only through one-off items: a £25m Capitalisation Direction, £16.048m Collection Fund Surplus, and contributions to reserves. When these temporary measures are removed, there remains a structural deficit of £39.048m that drives ongoing gaps of £33.098m (2027/28), £17.205m (2028/29), and beyond.
findings.matters: The council has not solved its budget problem; it has deferred it. The reliance on one-off capital direction and collection fund surpluses masks an unresolved structural imbalance between recurring costs and recurring revenue.
findings.figures: £39.048m structural gap from 2026/27; £25.000m Capitalisation Direction one-off; £16.048m Collection Fund Surplus one-off; £33.098m gap 2027/28 (before EFS)
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget includes net one-off items of £39.048m that do not contribute to the budget gap in future years... When these one-off items are removed, the structural gap from 2026/27 that needs to be addressed through the Medium Term Financial Plan is £39.048m.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s63304/Revenue and Capital Budget 2026-27 Council Tax 2026-27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 -.pdf
findings.headline: DSG High Needs deficit forecast to reach £217.229m by March 2028, with no confirmed government support for new deficits from 2026/27
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block deficit will hit £116.8m by March 2026 and £217.229m by 31 March 2028. Government will fund 90% of deficits accrued to March 2026 via a High Needs Stability Grant (£105.120m estimated), leaving £11.68m to be funded locally. However, there is no confirmed support for new deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 (estimated £100.429m). The statutory override that rings-fences this from General Fund reserves expires 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: This is a £217m contingent liability facing the council in two years. Failure to deliver the Deficit Management Plan or SEND reform targets could exhaust reserves and force a Section 114 Notice (effectively insolvency). Lenders need to understand this tail risk.
findings.figures: £116.800m by March 2026; £217.229m by 31 March 2028; £105.120m High Needs Stability Grant (90% of historical deficit); £11.680m local funding requirement; estimated £100.429m in new deficits 2026/27-2027/28
findings.quote: The DSG High Needs Block deficit is forecast to reach £116.800m by March 2026 and £217.229m by 31 March 2028... There is no confirmed Government support for deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28, this therefore remains a considerable risk... failure to do so could materially increase financial risk, exhaust reserves, and necessitate consideration of a Section 114 Notice.

findings.headline: Third consecutive year requiring exceptional financial support to achieve a balanced budget
findings.detail: Somerset has now needed government support in 2024/25, 2025/26, and 2026/27. The council is receiving a £25m Capitalisation Direction for 2026/27, plus an additional £5m for transformation. Despite savings of £21.836m and £50.261m in growth managed, the council cannot balance without this support.
findings.matters: A three-year pattern of subsidy indicates the council's cost base remains unaligned with sustainable revenue. This is not a one-off shock but structural deficit, making the council dependent on government discretion.
findings.figures: £25.000m Capitalisation Direction for 2026/27; third consecutive year of EFS; £45.017m-£45.777m approved savings over MTFP
findings.quote: Somerset Council has required a third year of Exceptional Financial Support to produce a balanced budget in 2026/27... It remains essential that the budget gap is addressed through permanent and sustainable action. Exceptional Financial Support cannot replace the need to reduce the cost base, strengthen income, and deliver the transformation required to achieve long term stability.

findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council has stabilised. Continued 'fragile' status two years later, with undefined and incomplete transformation plans, indicates ongoing financial distress without a clear exit strategy.

findings.quote: Although some of the additional controls have been stepped down or relaxed since then, the Council's financial position remains fragile. It must be addressed swiftly and robustly when agreeing the financial strategy for 2026/27 to 2030/31, which will need to be supported by further phases of large-scale service transformation to secure financial sustainability over the medium-term.

findings.headline: SEND system reforms depend on government White Paper (expected Autumn 2025) and funding settlement changes (announced November 2025), both of which are not yet published
findings.detail: The DMP explicitly depends on government policy changes that have not yet been announced. The paper states the council must 'focus upon the expected Government announcements in relation to SEND reform and addressing cumulative DSG deficits in the Autumn' and that 'Revisions to the management of SEND and DSG are likely to be necessary at this point.' The government's Fair Funding Review and SEND White Paper 'details of which will be set out in a White Paper in the Autumn' have not yet been published. If government policy changes materially, the DMP will need to be revised, potentially causing delays to delivery.
findings.matters: The DMP is built on assumptions about government policy that are not yet confirmed. If the government announces a different SEND funding model or deficit write-off scheme, the council's entire plan could require re-working. This is policy risk that is uncontrollable from the council's perspective.

findings.quote: The DMP will therefore need to be reviewed and revised periodically to take account of Government Policy changes. findings.headline: Exclusion and suspension rates for SEND pupils in Somerset are among the highest in England, indicating school system is struggling to retain pupils
findings.detail: The paper reports that 'Somerset had the fifth highest rate of exclusions of children with an EHCP in England and the second highest rate of suspensions of children with an EHCP.' In 2023/24, 147 pupils were permanently excluded (83 had SEND) and 3,716 pupils received one or more suspension (1,769 had SEND). High exclusion rates are both a symptom of unmet need and a cost driver, as excluded pupils often require costly alternative provision or INMS placements. A Joint Thematic Area Inspection noted that 'the low level of annual reviews being amended by the Council increases the risk that children at risk of serious youth violence who have Education Health and Care Plans may have plans that are not up to date.'
findings.matters: High exclusion/suspension rates suggest the mainstream system is breaking down and failing to meet pupils' needs, which drives them into more expensive provision. This is also a safeguarding risk for vulnerable pupils. If the DMP is to succeed, it must reverse this trend, which requires significant upstream investment.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s57909/Dedicated Schools Grant DSGDeficit Management Plan DMP.pdf
findings.headline: New investment of £1.945m required in 2026/27 to deliver DMP, with ongoing £1.722m commitment, to be funded from contingency budgets and future negotiations
findings.detail: To deliver the DMP, the council needs additional investment of £1.299m in 2025/26 (already approved by Executive, funded via corporate contingency), rising to £1.945m in 2026/27 with ongoing commitment of £1.722m. This includes £0.426m DSG High Needs Block growth and £0.455m-£0.679m General Fund growth for capacity in programme management, complaints/tribunals, and new roles. The 2025/26 investment was met from contingency; future years are to be 'addressed as part of balancing the 2026/27 budget in March 2026.' This means the council must find additional funding in an already stretched budget to fund deficit reduction.
findings.matters: Deficit reduction is not cost-free. The council must invest nearly £2m annually to achieve the savings, and this investment must come from a general fund that is itself projected to have a £101.384m deficit in 2026/27 and £190.041m by 2029/30. This is not a sustainable funding model.

findings.quote: Additional General Fund expenditure of £0.455m is required in the current year, with an ongoing commitment of £0.599m by 2027/28. There is potential for some of this investment to be funded via the Council's Transformation Programme through the use of Flexible Capital Receipts or the Capitalisation Direction in order to reduce the pressure upon mainstream budgets and reserves.

findings.headline: Independent Non-Maintained Schools (INMS) placements cost 10x more than mainstream provision but represent only 5% of SEND pupils, with costs consuming £20m more than mainstream support
findings.detail: The council notes that 'the average annual cost for an independent special school placement is more than 10 times higher than for a mainstream school. Somerset's budget for independent special school's places is £20m higher than its budget for mainstream school support.' Of 15,879 pupils with SEND, only 488 are in INMS settings (source: SEN2 data), yet INMS budget exceeds mainstream support budget by £20m. This indicates both a placement cost problem and a potential sign that mainstream schools are being inadequately resourced to keep pupils in-county, forcing more expensive out-of-county independent placements.
findings.matters: This is a cost structure problem. The council is paying premium prices for a small tail of placements, and the volume is rising. Without keeping more pupils in mainstream or council-run provision, the average cost per pupil will rise, making the deficit worse.
findings.figures: INMS placement cost: 10x mainstream cost; INMS budget £20m higher than mainstream support budget; INMS pupils 488 out of 15,879 SEND pupils (3%); total SEND pupils in state-funded schools: 13,306; total in independent schools: 2,573

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s57909/Dedicated Schools Grant DSGDeficit Management Plan DMP.pdf
findings.headline: Government statutory override expires 31 March 2028 with no announced solution for accumulated deficits, creating a compliance cliff
findings.detail: The government extended the DSG statutory override (which allows councils to hold accumulated DSG deficits separately from General Fund accounts) to 31 March 2028. However, the paper makes clear: 'this merely provides more time for local authorities to reduce their ongoing deficits and does not provide a solution to fund the cumulative deficits that have grown in recent years.' The council will still have a £129.437m cumulative deficit at March 2028, and no government policy has announced how or whether these deficits will be written off, restructured, or funded. Government reform plans and funding announcements are promised 'in the Autumn 2025' but have not yet been made.
findings.matters: The statutory override is what prevents a Section 114 notice today. When it expires, unless the government intervenes with a policy solution or funding injection, the council will be forced to issue a notice even if making steady progress on the DMP. This is a hard deadline risk that is entirely outside the council's control.
findings.figures: Statutory Override expires 31 March 2028; Projected cumulative deficit at that date: £129.437m (after DMP mitigation); Government's own analysis of DSG deficits nationally: 121 local authorities with cumulative deficits of £3.2 billion at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: Whilst the statutory override has recently been extended by Government from 31 March 2026 to 31 March 2028, this merely provides more time for local authorities to reduce their ongoing deficits and does not provide a solution to fund the cumulative deficits that have grown in recent years.

findings.headline: New DMP proposes £79.297m in savings by 2029/30 but delivery track record is poor and timescale is extremely tight
findings.detail: The council proposes to deliver £79.297m in cumulative savings by 2029/30 to move the budget into annual surplus (£2.911m) by 2028/29. However, this depends entirely on 'timely and effective delivery' of multiple complex projects including SEND units, Alternative Provision restructuring, funding banding review, and a digital finance system—all within 18 months to 3 years. Given that the first DMP 'has had limited impact', and many of these changes require further consultation and policy change (not yet approved), delivery risk is high. If savings fall short by even 20%, the deficit climbs back above £200m.
findings.matters: The entire mitigation strategy rests on achieving specific savings targets within a fixed timeframe. If delivery slips or assumptions prove wrong, there is no Plan B before the statutory override expires. Lenders need confidence in either realistic timelines or a fallback position.
findings.figures: £2.516m savings in 2025/26 (second half year only); £79.297m cumulative savings by 2029/30; Target of £56.841m savings by 2028/29 to achieve small surplus
findings.quote: The proposed DMP project workstreams have been subject to a thorough due diligence process conducted by Peopletoo, Finance and Education officers and are considered to represent reasonable cost reduction estimates subject to timely and effective delivery and implementation.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s57909/Dedicated Schools Grant DSGDeficit Management Plan DMP.pdf
findings.headline: SEND expenditure growth (27%) far outpacing DSG funding growth (16%) since pandemic, with placement demand forecast to surge 49% in five years
findings.detail: Since 2020/21, SEND expenditure has risen £58.123m (27%) while DSG funding has risen only £33.697m (16%), creating a structural funding gap that is the root cause of the deficit. More concerning, Full-Time Equivalent placements are forecast to grow from 4,727 in 2024/25 to 7,062 by 2029/30—a 49% increase in five years. This accelerating demand is the key cost driver and suggests the council will struggle to manage capacity and cost even with the new DMP in place.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled demand growth is the real risk. Even if the council delivers planned savings, if placement numbers continue to surge and average costs rise, the deficit will re-accelerate. This is not a one-time fix but a structural mismatch that will require ongoing intervention.
findings.figures: Expenditure growth 2020/21 to 2024/25: £58.123m (27%); DSG funding growth same period: £33.697m (16%); Placement FTE forecast growth 2024/25 to 2029/30: 4,727 to 7,062 (49% increase)
findings.quote: Since the Covid-19 pandemic, expenditure pressures have escalated from £213.080m in 2020/21 through to £271.203m in 2024/25, an increase of £58.123m (27%) as complexity of need has increased. DSG funding over this period has increased by £33.697m (16%).

findings.headline: Previous Deficit Management Plan has had limited impact and deficit continues to accelerate
findings.detail: The first DMP was produced in February 2024 but 'has had limited impact upon the Council's ability to manage and control its financial deficit to date, due to the length of time required to effect structural and systemic change.' The in-year deficit has actually widened from £28.081m in 2024/25 to a forecast £34.804m in 2025/26 and is projected to reach £57.835m by 2029/30. This acceleration despite interventions suggests the underlying demand and cost drivers are outpacing mitigation efforts.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG)/Deficit Management Plan (DMP)
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.somerset.gov.uk/documents/s57909/Dedicated Schools Grant DSGDeficit Management Plan DMP.pdf
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit projected to reach £294.6m by 2029/30 with Section 114 notice risk
findings.detail: The Council's DSG deficit has grown from £61.992m at 31 March 2025 to a projected £294.600m by 2029/30 under current policies. Without government support, this would require the Section 151 Officer to issue a Section 114 notice, which the paper explicitly states puts 'the Council at risk of the Section 151 Officer being required by law to issue a Section 114 Notice given that the Council's revenue reserves are insufficient to meet the projected shortfall of resources.' The statutory override providing temporary protection expires 31 March 2028, but even with the new DMP, a £129.437m cumulative deficit remains at that cliff-edge date.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration that a council cannot balance its budget and would severely restrict the council's ability to deliver services and borrow. For lenders, this is an existential risk to the council's financial viability.
findings.figures: £61.992m deficit at 31 March 2025; £294.600m projected by 2029/30; £129.437m deficit remaining at 31 March 2028 when statutory override expires; current revenue reserves insufficient to meet projected shortfall
findings.quote: This presents a significant strategic financial risk to the Council's financial sustainability and puts the Council at risk of the Section 151 Officer being required by law to issue a Section 114 Notice given that the Council's revenue reserves are insufficient to meet the projected shortfall of resources.
